conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screening that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. It helps us understand what support might be most helpful for you now that your baby is here.

Everything you share stays confidential within our team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just your honest experience. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause or stop.

I’ll ask each question conversationally; you answer however feels easiest for you. Ready to begin?

First, how often in the past week have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Good morning. Yes, I’m ready.

I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but I do find things funny most days. I’d say I laugh and see the humorous side pretty regularly.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, most days I can still laugh—maybe not every single moment, but I definitely still find things funny and can enjoy a good chuckle when something silly happens.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yeah, I do look forward to things—like having coffee with a friend or taking the baby for a walk. I still get that little spark of excitement when I plan something I enjoy.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If the baby’s fussy or I’m running late, I might think, “Could I have done something differently?” but I don’t stay stuck on it. I figure babies are unpredictable, and I’m doing my best, so I don’t beat myself up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah—like I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing when he’s napping, even though I just checked on him. It’s not constant, but every now and then my mind jumps to “what-ifs” for no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—just a quick rush of worry every so often, like when he’s quiet in the car seat and I imagine something’s wrong. It passes in a minute and I can settle myself, so I wouldn’t call it scared or panicky.
Things have been getting on top of me

A little bit, maybe. Some days the feedings and laundry pile up and I feel a bit swamped, but it’s not overwhelming. I usually make a quick list, tackle one thing at a time, and feel back on track before the day’s over.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened. I’ve been sleeping fine—well, as fine as any new mom can with night feedings. I’m tired, but I drift off pretty easily once the baby settles.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I have moments where I feel a bit weepy if I’m extra tired, but it’s short-lived. Overall I still feel pretty upbeat.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried from unhappiness. Maybe a tear or two when I was super exhausted last week, but it was more about being tired than feeling sad.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. That thought hasn’t crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety (EPDS proxy)

Patient-reported symptoms  
- Mild, situational worry about infant safety (Q4, Q5) – no pervasive panic.  
- Occasional “weeps” when fatigued; denies persistent sadness, crying spells, or anhedonia (Q7–Q9).  
- Denies guilt/self-blame (Q3) and self-harm ideation (Q10).  
- Maintains capacity for enjoyment and laughter (Q1, Q2).  
- Endorses transient “getting on top of me” feeling, but manageable with planning (Q6).

Pattern  
Transient, fatigue-related distress without sustained low mood, functional impairment, or safety concerns.

Screening significance  
Current responses do not suggest elevated risk for postpartum depression or anxiety; no safety flags identified. Continue routine postpartum monitoring and re-screen if mood or functioning deteriorates.
